extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of medieval/Crusades history
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly narrative account and analysis of the First Crusade and the early Latin kingdom of Jerusalem (c.1097–1143), emphasizing political, military, religious and economic factors that shaped events and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: the aims of the adventurer prince
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the princes who joined the First Crusade there were some who were rather politiques than devots, and who aimed at the acquisition of temporal profit as well as of spiritual merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political ambition of leaders (e.g., Bohemund, Baldwin, Raymond) shaped decisions on where to campaign, what to besiege, and the founding of principalities (Antioch, Edessa, Tripoli); jealousy and competing projects among princes affected unity and progress of the crusade.

rubrics_metrics.name: interests of the Italian merchant
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of the Italian towns (Genoa, Venice, Pisa) and their merchants was important in supplying ships, provisions and siege-material, and later in enabling and shaping the foundation and expansion of the kingdom of Jerusalem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial motives affected strategic choices and governance: Italian fleets supplied provisions, siege-tackle and naval support; merchants demanded privileges (freedom from tolls, quarters, shares of booty and city concessions) in return, which in turn shaped political and territorial development of Frankish states.

rubrics_metrics.name: policy of the Greeks (Alexius' homage policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alexius I. induced the crusader leaders to do him homage so that conquests would be held as his vassals rather than by independent crusader princes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book contrasts Alexius' policy with an alternative: he could have treated the crusaders as independent allies and divided conquests cooperatively. His insistence on homage produced resentment, long-term mistrust between East and West, helped sour relations (contributing to later events like 1204), and complicated crusader governance and territorial ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: condition of the Mahommedan East (disunion and dynastic fragmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disunion among Syrian amirs, division between Abbasids and Fatimites, and the political fragmentation of Seljuk authority made the region vulnerable and largely explains crusader success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Muslim polities were divided or distracted by internecine warfare, the crusaders could exploit rivalries and gain allies or neutrality; conversely, when a unifying power (e.g., under Zengi or Saladin) arose, Latin Christian fortunes declined rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: sea-power and maritime support
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea-power (Italian ships) influenced the crusaders' victory by supplying provisions, munitions and siege matériel, and by assisting in sieges (Antioch, Jerusalem) and coastal operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control of ports and access to naval support was a strategic advantage: Genoese, Venetian and Pisan fleets provided critical logistical and military assistance in return for commercial privileges. Maritime allies could determine which towns were sustainable and profitable to hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: nature of Seljuk occupation (military rather than administrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seljuk occupation of Asia Minor and Syria was often a military occupation (garrisons, armies) without deep administrative penetration; towns' inhabitants were frequently hostile to garrisons and wide tracts were sparsely garrisoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A superficially held territory with hostile populace and weak civil control is easier for an invading, mobile force to traverse and conquer; this explains the relative ease of the crusaders' advance after key victories like Nicaea and Dorylaeum.

rubrics_metrics.name: political fragmentation after Malik Shah's death
rubrics_metrics.description: After Malik Shah (1092) the Seljuk empire dissolved into independent regional rulers (e.g., Kilij Arslan in Konia), weakening centralized resistance to the crusaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power fragmentation produced multiple independent centres (Konya, Sivas, Mosul, Aleppo, etc.) whose rivalries reduced coordinated defence and allowed crusader forces to exploit gaps and form local alliances (e.g., with Armenian principalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: religious fervour and spiritual phenomena as morale factors
rubrics_metrics.description: During periods of extreme stress spiritualistic phenomena (e.g., the discovery of the Holy Lance) appeared and could dramatically raise morale, helping the crusaders to withstand sieges or defeat relief armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charismatic religious events could reorient political influence within the crusader leadership (e.g., Raymund's prominence after the Lance) and temporarily unite or energize troops; but leaders and sceptics could also view such phenomena instrumentally in political struggles.

rubrics_metrics.name: church vs state in deciding governance of conquered Jerusalem
rubrics_metrics.description: After the capture of Jerusalem a contest arose over whether the city should be governed ecclesiastically (theocracy under the patriarch) or as a lay feudal kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence/absence of strong church leadership (death of Bishop Adhemar) and the composition of the army/pilgrims determined the outcome; institutional capacity and leadership personalities influenced whether a theocratic or secular regime emerged (resulting in Baldwin I's kingship rather than a patriarchal dominion).

rubrics_metrics.name: economic motives dictating territorial expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic and commercial motives (control of ports, trade routes, caravan routes to Red Sea and Egypt) significantly dictated the expansion and shape of the Latin kingdom, often alongside religious motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial acquisitions (coastal strip from Beirut to el-Arish, southern extensions to Red Sea ports, fortresses controlling caravan routes) often had clear commercial rationales, and the kingdom's strength and longevity depended on such economic connections and concessions to maritime republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: alliances with neighbouring powers (Damascus, Constantinople) as survival factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Alliances or enmities with nearby powers—viziers and amirs of Damascus, emperors of Constantinople—were decisive in determining the kingdom's fortunes against rising Muslim powers like Zengi and later Nureddin/Saladin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic diplomacy (e.g., alliance with Damascus under Muin-eddin Anar) could provide vital allies against unifying Muslim forces; conversely, breaches of alliances (e.g., the Second Crusade's attack on Damascus) removed potential supports and hastened decline.
